newsitem.title: UK: Sterling boosted as firm data fuel rate rise talk.
newsitem.headline: Sterling boosted as firm data fuel rate rise talk.

text.p: Rising British October retail sales and a 10.3 percent jump in broad money supply growth revealed on Wednesday will boost an already robust pound as they stoke market speculation of rate rises, analysts said.
The 0.4 percent month-on-month retail sales increase matched forecasts but the three-month leap of 4.0 percent versus the same period a year ago was the largest rise in over two years.
"The upward pressure on interest rates is still there, and therefore the upward pressure on the currency is still there," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
The headline retail sales rise masked strong growth in textile, clothing and footwear sales, where prices had already risen strongly in recent months, analysts noted.

The sales figure did nothing, therefore, to dilute the tightening implications of the big October M4 rise and a hefty 7.4 billion sterling ($12.4 billion) leap in bank and building society lending, they said.

Sterling remained firm after the data, trading at 2.5198 marks and $1.6785 at European midsession versus 2.5176 and $1.6760 in Europe late Tuesday. It earlier hit $1.6820, its best level since October 1992, and a 30-month peak of 2.5260 marks.

The market spotlight is now on the next monetary meeting between Bank of England governor Eddie George and Chancellor Kenneth Clarke on December 11, with speculation intensifying that interest rates will be hiked then.
Rates were raised by a quarter-point on October 30.

"Despite sterling strength and the rate rise on October 30, there is a continued feeling that policy is too loose and ought to be tightened, and there's a feeling the Chancellor may well do it," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
"To that extent it ought to be a small positive for sterling," he added.
Wednesday's figures came hot on the heels of Monday's data showing a flood of corporate tax receipts helped the government repay a chunky 4.393 billion sterling of public debt in October.
It helped soothe market fears that the Chancellor might unveil economically-imprudent tax cuts in next Tuesday's budget.
The Conservative government, trailing in opinion polls and facing a general election which must be held by next May, has made no secret of its desire to make vote-wooing tax giveaways.
But the market is now more relaxed that Clarke will announce modest tax cuts, while lowering spending and public borrowing.
Members of parliament's Treasury Select Committee back economists' predictions. They told Reuters they expect a prudent budget and a penny cut off income tax -- as does the market.

"What the (October 30) interest rate rise shows is that his budget is going to be a cautious budget. It's not going to be an electioneering budget," said Matthew Carrington, the Conservative chairman of the panel.
Analysts said a tight budget package might allow Clarke to resist Bank of England calls for monetary tightening.
Foreign investors and the bond market are likely to welcome a prudent budget, and that would please a pound which is already at more than four-year trade-weighted highs, analysts said.
But some believed even a bigger tax giveaway would support the currency, as it would throw the focus again on interest rate increases -- music to the ears of yield-hungry investors.
"It's almost a win-win scenario for sterling," said CIBC's Coleman. ($1=.5950 Pound)
